details: ICRP 108 (2008) Environmental Protection: Reference Animals and Plants (RAPs); established 12 reference organisms for dose rate assessment; screening values (mGy/day): below which no population-level effects expected: whole organism dose rates <1 mGy/day for most organisms; 1-10 mGy/day: minor effects possible; >10 mGy/day: significant population effects likely; ICRP defined reference organisms: deer, rat, duck, frog, trout, flatfish, bee, earthworm, crab, pine tree, wild grass, seaweed
ecological_significance: ICRP 108 framework applied to CEZ: dose rates in most CEZ areas <1 mGy/day for representative mammals → below screening value; higher dose rates in hot spots (near Red Forest burial sites); demonstrates: CEZ wildlife thriving at ambient dose rates (see Deryabina 2015; cez_wildlife_population_census_REAL.csv) because ambient doses generally below ICRP 108 screening levels; individual hot spots may exceed levels but population-level wildlife not affected
source: ICRP 108 2008; Beresford 2022; UNSCEAR 2008 Annex E; Copplestone 2011 J Radiol Prot

details: External + internal dose rate to deer (Capreolus capreolus) in CEZ: external: from Cs-137 in soil (dominant pathway in forest); at 100 kBq/m² Cs-137 external dose rate to deer ~0.01-0.05 mGy/day; internal: from ingestion of grass/bark/mushrooms contaminated with Cs-137 and Sr-90; total dose rate typical CEZ deer: 0.03-3.0 mGy/day depending on habitat; most CEZ habitats: deer dose rate 0.1-1 mGy/day
ecological_significance: Deer dose rate 0.1-1 mGy/day: within ICRP 108 range where minor effects possible but population-level effects not expected; consistent with Deryabina 2015 finding of normal deer population density in CEZ; note: dose rate to deer from Cs-137 body burden (internal) approximately equals external dose from soil Cs-137 in typical CEZ habitats; both pathways contribute roughly equally to total dose
source: cez_wildlife_population_census_REAL.csv; Beresford 2022; ICRP 108; Barnett 2006 J Radiol Prot

details: Dose rate to soil organisms in CEZ: earthworms (direct contact with contaminated soil; ingest ~50g soil/day): dose rate = external from soil + ingestion of Cs-137 and Sr-90; at 100 kBq/m² Cs-137: earthworm dose rate ~0.5-5 mGy/day; Red Forest (4000-10000 kBq/m²): earthworm dose rate potentially 20-100 mGy/day (above ICRP 108 screening value of 10 mGy/day); pine trees in Red Forest in 1986: received thousands of mGy (caused browning and death)
ecological_significance: Red Forest trees = only clearly radiation-killed biota from Chernobyl; dose rates in Red Forest 1986: estimated >50 Gy total to trees (acute + chronic) → cell death in needles; bark; cambium; trees died and turned rust-red (hence 'Red Forest'); earthworms in Red Forest 1986: likely received lethal doses; recovered by 1990s as dose rates declined; ICRP 108 allows site-specific assessment; most CEZ habitats now below screening values

details: Dose rate to catfish in ZNPP cooling pond: body burden Cs-137 ~96,000 Bq/kg wet weight (see cez_wildlife_contamination_REAL.csv); assuming 30 kg catfish: total body activity = 2.88×10⁶ Bq Cs-137; internal dose rate from Cs-137 = activity × dose coefficient; whole-body dose rate ~0.01-0.1 mGy/day internal; external from surrounding water (Cs-137 in water ~5-20 Bq/L): ~0.001 mGy/day; total: ~0.01-0.1 mGy/day; plus Sr-90 internal component
ecological_significance: Catfish total dose rate 0.01-0.1 mGy/day: below ICRP 108 fish screening value of 1 mGy/day; consistent with thriving catfish population in cooling pond; at 96,000 Bq/kg body burden: fish experiencing real internal irradiation but not at population-harmful level; individual physiological effects (chromosomal abnormalities documented) present but not preventing population; threshold of effect vs population extinction = different criteria

details: Dose rate to plants (wild grass) in typical CEZ: external gamma from Cs-137 in soil (primary pathway); at 100 kBq/m² Cs-137: grass external dose rate ~0.01 mGy/day; internal from root uptake: small (Cs-137 plant uptake low in most soils); total: ~0.01-0.1 mGy/day for typical CEZ meadow; pine tree (conifer): higher surface area + wax cuticle traps more alpha particles + more canopy interception of fallout → pine external dose rate ~2-5x grass in same location
ecological_significance: Plant dose rates in CEZ: generally well below ICRP 108 screening values for plants (10 mGy/day); forest trees in Red Forest in 1986 exceeded this threshold massively; by 1990: Red Forest trees receiving <1 mGy/day and regenerating; current Red Forest: successor deciduous trees (birch, poplar) growing normally because dose rates now well below screening level; deciduous better than conifer because: shorter exposure season; waxy deciduous leaves trap less contamination

details: ERICA (Environmental Risk from Ionising Contaminants: Assessment and Management) tool: EU-developed software for environmental dose assessment; calculates dose rates to organisms from: radionuclide concentrations in environmental media; concentration ratios (CR); organism geometry; accounts for external + internal pathways; ICRP 108 RAPs built into ERICA; validated against CEZ wildlife data; used for regulatory assessment of nuclear sites across EU
ecological_significance: ERICA model applied to CEZ: Beresford 2022 (Chernobyl Environmental Evaluation) used ERICA to calculate dose rates for 44 wildlife taxa across 5 habitat types; conclusions: most taxa and habitats at <1 mGy/day (below ICRP 108 screening); highest dose rates in Red Forest interior and near burial sites; wildlife populations in low-dose CEZ habitats showing no population-level effects (supporting ICRP 108 screening approach validity)
source: Beresford 2022; ERICA tool documentation; ICRP 108; cez_wildlife_population_census_REAL.csv; cez_ecosystem_ecology_REAL.csv

details: Natural radiation dose rate to typical terrestrial organism: external gamma from terrestrial background + cosmic rays: ~0.001-0.005 mGy/day in typical temperate region; Ramsar Iran: ~0.05-0.5 mGy/day (due to Ra-228 high natural background); deep sea hydrothermal vents: ~10 mGy/day from volcanic radioactivity; CEZ current (2026): 0.01-1.0 mGy/day for typical organism → 2-200x natural background; Red Forest: ~1-10 mGy/day → 200-2000x natural background
ecological_significance: Natural background evolution: all life on Earth evolved with radiation dose rates ~0.001-0.01 mGy/day; organisms have DNA repair machinery evolved for this rate; DNA repair saturates at higher rates; at ICRP 108 screening values (~1 mGy/day): DNA repair can compensate; above ~10 mGy/day: cumulative unrepaired damage leads to population effects; this framework explains why CEZ has thriving wildlife at 0.01-1 mGy/day but Red Forest 1986 trees died at >50 mGy/day
source: ICRP 108; natural_background_radiation_REAL.csv; Tubiana 2005 Radiat Res; radiation_biology_mechanisms_REAL.csv

details: CEZ biota radionuclide inventory (2026 approximate): forest soil surface (0-5cm) in typical CEZ forest: Cs-137 ~50-500 kBq/m²; Sr-90 ~5-50 kBq/m²; Pu-239+240 ~0.1-10 kBq/m²; Am-241 ~0.5-5 kBq/m²; total alpha-emitter activity INCREASING as Am-241 grows from Pu-241; Am-241 now exceeds Pu-239+240 in many locations (t½ 432yr vs decay of 24,110yr precursor); see am241_ingrowth_timeseries_REAL.csv for trajectory
ecological_significance: Am-241 now ecologically most significant growing alpha contaminant: in 1986: Pu-239+240 dominated alpha activity; in 2026: Am-241 equals or exceeds Pu-239+240 in many locations; by 2058: Am-241 activity peaks at 82.7 TBq total (see Bateman equations in am241_ingrowth_timeseries_REAL.csv); Am-241 59.54 keV gamma becoming increasingly detectable; as Cs-137 decays to background (~2120), Am-241 will be dominant long-lived gamm+alpha source

details: Chronic radiation effects in CEZ wildlife (contested): Moller Mousseau 2011 (barn swallows; Hirundo rustica): claimed elevated frequency of partial albinism; tumor-like growths; abnormal sperm morphology in swallows from contaminated CEZ areas; challenged by: Baker 2016; Deryabina 2015; other independent analyses; UNSCEAR 2021: acknowledged Moller/Mousseau findings but questioned methodology; found insufficient evidence for population-level effects in any vertebrate species at current CEZ dose rates
ecological_significance: Scientific consensus (2026): individual-level genetic effects plausible at higher CEZ dose rates (barn swallows may receive >1 mGy/day in some areas); population-level effects not confirmed in large vertebrates; species-specific variation expected; swallows are aerial insect feeders = different exposure than ground-feeding species; Moller/Mousseau methodology disputes center on: selection of contaminated vs control sites; correction for other environmental variables; sample sizes; Baker 2016 independent replication key counter-evidence
source: contested_radiation_science_REAL.csv; Baker 2016 PLOS ONE; Moller Mousseau 2011 Ecol Lett doi:10.1111/j.1461-0248.2011.01618.x; UNSCEAR 2021; cez_wildlife_population_census_REAL.csv
